passage: On the kitchen floor sat four toddlers, each with a plastic box they could not open. Swati twisted the lid, pulled it, banged it on the tiles and poked at its edge with one finger. Every move lasted a few seconds and was dropped when nothing gave. Vidya had seen her father unscrew his tiffin box that morning. She copied the turning motion of his wrist on a small pack of raisins, but she turned it in the opposite direction, so the cover stayed put. Sarika's lid would not budge either. Her face went red, she hurled the box towards the wall and screamed, and there was no more trying after that. Little Rohan had once popped a box open by pressing its corner, purely by chance. Now he pressed at each lid's corner, and was baffled when a bottle with a screw cap did nothing at all.

qa.q: What did Vidya copy from her father?
qa.a: She copied the twisting motion of his wrist on the lid.

qa.q: How does Sarika's reaction differ from Swati's, and what did each do with the lid?
qa.a: Swati kept trying different moves for a few seconds each, so she kept exploring. Sarika's strong feeling made her throw the box and scream, which ended any trying.

qa.q: What was Rohan probably feeling when the screw-top bottle did nothing?
qa.a: He was puzzled, since pressing the corner had worked on earlier boxes and now it did not.

qa.q: How could a caregiver support Sarika when the lid will not open?
qa.a: A caregiver could stay near, name the upset feeling calmly, and show one way to try again or help with the first turn, so the trying can start again. 🙂

grounding: Four toddlers try to open a plastic box by trial and error, imitation, giving way to frustration, and repeating a move that once worked.

passage: Four groups of students on the same school trip fund each had a different plan. Charu's group started with a total of three thousand rupees per person, took away transport and the place to stay, and saw that only about eight hundred was left for food and tickets. Chinmay's group weighed a sleeper train, a coach and a cab shared with others for price, travel time and safety. They took the sleeper for the night journey and accepted that it would be slower, to save money. Omkar's group crammed eight places into two days. Worn out by all the travelling, they skipped half of them and still paid for tickets they never used, because nobody had thought about how slowly people actually move. Nisha's group found the hostel they wanted was full. They phoned two other places, chose one once a parent agreed, trimmed the food budget to pay for it, and updated the shared plan.

qa.q: How much was left for food and tickets in Charu's group?
qa.a: About eight hundred was left.

qa.q: How did Omkar's group's plan differ from Chinmay's group's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Omkar's group crammed eight places into two days and had to skip half while paying for unused tickets. Chinmay's group compared transport by cost, time and safety and picked the train for the overnight leg.

qa.q: What might Omkar's group be feeling after skipping half the places?
qa.a: They are probably tired and disappointed, and perhaps annoyed about the wasted ticket money.

qa.q: What could Omkar's group do differently next time?
qa.a: They could choose fewer places and allow travel time between them, then check the plan against the budget. A short list that they can enjoy is better than a long one. 🙂

grounding: Four groups plan a budget trip by working backward from a total, comparing options, overpacking, and replanning after a booking falls through.

passage: An email arrived saying that a shopping app had been breached, and four users each reacted differently. Manjula changed her password there, and on every other site that had shared it, then turned on a second step for logging in. Salma's card number had been part of the leak. She rang the bank on the number that appears on the card itself, not one from a message, blocked the card and asked about alerts on transactions. Dolma thought the email looked like junk and deleted it. Weeks later, calls began to arrive from people who knew her details and pretended to be from the bank. The delay made it harder to trace where they had come from. Aarav saw a payment he did not recognise. He moved from prevention to reporting: he told the bank, filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal, wrote to the app, and kept screenshots of everything.

qa.q: Which number did Salma use to call the bank?
qa.a: She used the number printed on her card.

qa.q: How does Dolma's response to the email differ from Manjula's, and what happened?
qa.a: Dolma deleted the email, and weeks later callers used her details. Manjula changed passwords everywhere she reused one and turned on a second login step, limiting further harm.

qa.q: What might Aarav be feeling when he sees the payment he does not recognise?
qa.a: He is probably worried and alarmed, and that pushed him to report it quickly.

qa.q: What should Dolma do now that suspicious calls have begun?
qa.a: She should not share any details on those calls, contact her bank using the number on her card, change her passwords, and report the calls through the official channels. 🤍

grounding: Four users respond to a data breach notice by securing accounts, contacting the bank, ignoring the email, and reporting misuse once it appears.

passage: Just before the maths test, a friend whispered to Kalyani, "Let me copy yours." She said no, and promised to go through the method once school ended, and they stayed friends. Noor was asked the same thing and worked it out in his head. Copying would give a mark but no learning, and the next chapter would leave him lost, so helping his friend copy was not really helping. Aman showed his answers because he feared his friend would stop talking to him. Afterwards he worried all evening, since the teacher might blame both of them, and the worry only grew. Kabir said no twice. Then he heard that his friend planned to bring a small chit into the exam. He went to the teacher privately after school and told them, because stopping something bigger seemed worth it. The teacher thanked him, said the friend would be spoken to that same day, and asked Kabir not to worry.

qa.q: Whom did the friend whisper to before the maths test?
qa.a: The friend whispered to Kalyani.

qa.q: How does Aman's choice differ from Kalyani's, and what did each feel afterwards?
qa.a: Aman gave in to keep his friend and worried afterwards. Kalyani said no and offered help after class, and they stayed friends.

qa.q: What was Aman feeling that evening, and why?
qa.a: Aman was anxious and afraid, because the teacher might blame both of them and his fear kept growing.

qa.q: What could Aman do to put things right?
qa.a: He could tell his friend he was wrong to share the answers, and talk to the teacher or a parent about what happened. Offering to explain the method instead would be a better way to help.

grounding: Children answer a friend's wish to copy by refusing kindly, thinking about what a test is for, giving in from fear, and telling the teacher when it will not stop.

passage: Parul planted tulsi and marigold in empty tins and watered them every morning before school, pressing a finger into the soil to check whether it was still damp. Amandeep went to the nursery man and learned that chilli loves sun while mint prefers shade, so he set one pot by the window and another beside the wall. Ishaan believed that more water meant faster growth. He poured it over his seedlings again and again all day, until the roots rotted, the leaves yellowed and the plants drooped. Bhavna's rose was doing well until an afternoon of fierce heat turned its leaves crisp. She carried the pot to a spot with partial shade and spread dry leaves over the soil to keep the moisture in. A week later the new leaves were green.

qa.q: What did Parul use as pots for her tulsi and marigold?
qa.a: She used empty tins.

qa.q: How does Ishaan's way of watering differ from Parul's, and what happened to each plant?
qa.a: Ishaan poured water several times a day and the roots rotted, while Parul checked the soil with a finger before watering. Her plants stayed healthy.

qa.q: What might Ishaan be feeling as he sees the leaves yellow?
qa.a: He is probably confused and disappointed, since he was trying hard to help the seedlings grow faster.

qa.q: What could Ishaan do to save the next batch of seedlings?
qa.a: He could check the soil with a finger like Parul and ask the nursery man how much each plant needs. Watering a little at a time is better than more. 🙂

grounding: Children look after a small garden with a daily routine, learning each plant's needs, overwatering, and moving a plant out of the sun.

passage: Four teams were building science models for the fair, and each leader steered differently. Nilesh's team wrote down research, materials, building and presentation, gave each member the job that suited their strengths, and set a date for every stage. Jaya, another leader, saw that painting could not begin until the frame dried and that testing needed a circuit that already worked. So she started those linked jobs first and let the separate ones run beside them. Deepak trusted nobody with the work. He did most of it at night and grew exhausted, the team felt pushed aside, the quality fell, and the others learned nothing from the project. After the model failed at the fair, Meena asked each member to name one worry. She then scored the ideas for money, hours and whether they could be done, so the next decision rested on evidence rather than on who sounded most sure.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's team set for every stage?
qa.a: They set a date for every stage.

qa.q: How does Deepak's way of leading differ from Nilesh's, and what happened to the teams?
qa.a: Deepak did most of the work himself, so he was exhausted, quality fell and the team learned nothing. Nilesh gave each member a task that matched their strengths and set dates, so everyone took part.

qa.q: What might the members of Deepak's team be feeling?
qa.a: They probably feel sidelined and unimportant, because Deepak did the work himself and did not trust them.

qa.q: What could Deepak try to work better with his team?
qa.a: He could give each member a clear job, check in on progress, and listen to their concerns, as Meena did. Sharing the work would also stop him being exhausted. 🙂

grounding: Team leaders manage a group project by assigning tasks, ordering dependent work, doing everything alone, and inviting concerns to decide by criteria.
